passage:
I've shared a flat with Ishita since August, and she agrees with everyone. "Love the curry!" to our flatmate across the hall, who burns everything. "No, the music doesn't bother me," to the boy upstairs, even the night before her exam. "That haircut really suits you." "Sure, I'll come," and then a late message saying she's unwell.
On her birthday, after the others left, she sat on the balcony with a paper plate of cake and didn't eat it. She asked me, quite quietly, "Kalyani, do people actually like me, or do they just like that I never say no?" I didn't know what to answer. I'm not sure she knows what she really likes either. I told her I'd rather hear her real opinion about my curry, even if it stings.

qa.q: What did Ishita say to the boy upstairs about his music?
qa.a: She said, "No, the music doesn't bother me," even the night before her exam.

qa.q: What does Ishita's question on the balcony suggest she is worried about?
qa.a: It suggests she worries that people like only her agreeableness, not her real self, because her many polite untruths hide what she thinks.

qa.q: What small step could Ishita take to rebuild real trust with the people she lives with?
qa.a: She could start giving small honest opinions kindly, like telling Kalyani what she really thinks of the curry, so her yes and no mean something again.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Ishita's constant agreeing?
qa.a: Kalyani finds it makes Ishita hard to know and would rather hear an honest opinion, even if it stings.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young woman whose steady stream of polite falsehoods leaves her unsure who really likes her.

passage:
First Sunday. Shalini planned a sunrise trek for their college group. Lavanya hates early mornings and steep paths. "Sounds amazing, count me in," she typed.
Ten days later. Lavanya gave her seminar talk, and Shalini said, "That was so good." Lavanya smiled and thanked her, but one thought kept coming back on the walk to the hostel: how would I even know? I say "so good" about everything. Maybe everyone does. She couldn't think of one person whose praise she was sure of.
The next Saturday, sitting on a rock halfway up the hill, sweaty and cold, she finally said it. "Shalini, honestly, I don't like treks. I kept saying yes." Shalini burst out laughing. "I only planned it because you said it sounded amazing!" They walked down together and found a tea stall instead.

qa.q: What did Lavanya type when Shalini planned the sunrise trek?
qa.a: Lavanya typed, "Sounds amazing, count me in."

qa.q: Why did the praise for the seminar talk leave Lavanya uneasy?
qa.a: Lavanya realised she says "so good" about everything, so she felt unsure whether anyone's praise, including Shalini's, was real.

qa.q: Which choice on the trek helped, and why?
qa.a: Lavanya admitted she doesn't like treks and had kept saying yes; that honest sentence cleared the confusion and they found something both enjoyed.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had said no to the trek on the first Sunday?
qa.a: Shalini might never have planned it, and both of them could have skipped a cold, uncomfortable morning.

grounding: Over a few weeks a young woman sees that her habit of polite yeses leaves her unable to trust anyone's praise, and one honest sentence starts to fix it.

passage:
On the night before Jasleen's birthday, her flatmates in the Pune flat were planning a surprise, and Uma knocked on her door to ask one thing.
"What do you actually like to eat? Honestly."
Jasleen opened her mouth to say "anything is fine" and stopped. For eight months she had told Uma her rajma was the best, told the other girls she loved their loud music, said yes to every film and every plan. Each time it had felt polite. Harmless.
"You always say you love everything," Uma said, not unkindly. "So we don't know. We don't really know you."
Jasleen sat on the bed. She realised she didn't know them either. Did they invite her because they liked her, or because she never said no?
"Momos," she said finally. "And I hate that music. I'm sorry."
Uma burst out laughing. "Finally. Hello, Jasleen."

qa.q: What did Jasleen finally say she likes to eat?
qa.a: She said "Momos."

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she sat on the bed?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and a bit lonely, because she realised that after months of polite yeses she could not tell whether her flatmates really liked her.

qa.q: What could Jasleen try in the flat from now on?
qa.a: She could keep small kindnesses but share her real likes and dislikes, so her friendships rest on who she actually is.

qa.q: How does Uma see Jasleen's constant agreement?
qa.a: Uma finds it hard to get close to her, since always saying "I love it" means the flatmates never really know her.

grounding: It shows a young adult whose steady stream of polite falsehoods leaves her unsure who really likes her, and one honest moment that starts to repair trust.

passage:
"So you're coming to Goa with my cousins?" Yash asked, dropping onto his hostel bed.
"Yeah, sure, sounds great," said Jagdish.
"You said that about the trek too. And then you were sick the whole time."
"I liked the trek."
"You told me you hate mountains. In October."
Jagdish laughed awkwardly. "Did I?"
"Bro, you say yes to everything. You said you loved my biryani. You don't even eat mutton."
Jagdish went quiet. "I just didn't want to make it a thing."
"It's not a thing. It's just… I don't know when you mean it." Yash sat up. "When you say you like hanging out with me, is that also just polite?"
"No! That one's true."
"How would I know?"
Jagdish stared at the ceiling fan. "Honestly? I don't want to go to Goa. I'd rather stay here and actually talk to you."

qa.q: Which dish did Jagdish claim to love, according to Yash?
qa.a: The biryani Yash made.

qa.q: What might Yash be worried about when he asks if hanging out is "just polite"?
qa.a: Yash is worried and a little hurt, afraid that even Jagdish's friendship might be another polite yes rather than something real.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Many small polite yeses made Jagdish's words unreliable; saying his true preferences, like skipping Goa, helps rebuild trust.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see the habit of agreeing at first?
qa.a: At first Jagdish sees it as avoiding fuss and keeping things easy, not as something that makes Yash doubt him.

grounding: It shows a young adult's many polite falsehoods to a roommate adding up until the friend cannot tell what is real.

passage:
I'm Tejas, and it took me most of first year to notice what I was doing.
I told the girl next door her paintings were brilliant. I told the guys on my floor I loved their gaming nights. I told the seniors their band was great. I said "same here" to every opinion in the mess. None of it felt like lying. It felt like being easy to be around.
Then, one night in March, Farhan asked me, "Out of all of us, who do you actually enjoy spending time with?" I opened my mouth, and nothing came. I honestly didn't know anymore. Worse, I didn't know who liked me, the real me, because I had never shown anyone.
Since then I've been trying something small. Once a day, I say one true thing, even a tiny one: "I don't like horror films." It feels strange. People haven't run away.

qa.q: When did Farhan ask the question?
qa.a: He asked it one night in March.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he couldn't answer Farhan's question?
qa.a: Tejas felt shaken and empty, realising the constant polite agreement had hidden who Tejas really was, even from Tejas.

qa.q: What small step is Tejas trying now?
qa.a: Tejas says one true thing a day, even a tiny one, which slowly lets people meet the real person and rebuilds trust.

qa.q: What might Farhan have noticed that led him to ask his question?
qa.a: Farhan may have noticed that Tejas agreed with everyone about everything, which made it hard to know what Tejas actually enjoyed.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing that many small polite falsehoods have left the narrator unsure who really likes them.

passage:
Student counsellor's note, Thursday
Jomon (second year) came in saying he feels "weirdly lonely" in a flat of five friends.
As we talked, a pattern appeared. He tells his flatmate Manjula he loves her cooking when he doesn't. He says "no problem" when people borrow his laptop, and it is a problem. He laughs at jokes he finds mean. He said, "I just want everyone to be comfortable."
Then he said something important: "But now I don't know if any of them actually like me, or just the version that agrees with everything."
I told him a kind fib now and then does no harm, but when it becomes the only way he speaks, nobody gets to know the real Jomon. We picked one small true thing to try this week: telling Manjula, kindly, that he'd rather she asked before borrowing his charger.
He looked nervous, but agreed. We'll meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: What does Jomon tell Manjula about her cooking?
qa.a: He tells her he loves her cooking when he doesn't.

qa.q: How is Jomon feeling in the flat, and why?
qa.a: Jomon feels weirdly lonely, unsure whether anyone likes the real him or only the version that agrees with everything.

qa.q: What small step did the counsellor and Jomon choose?
qa.a: Telling Manjula kindly that he'd rather she asked before borrowing his charger, one small true thing to try that week.

qa.q: How might Manjula react if Jomon starts saying what he really thinks?
qa.a: Manjula might be surprised at first, but could come to know and trust the real Jomon better.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose many small polite untruths have left him unsure who really likes him, as noted by a counsellor.
